item.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=robustness+observer+agreement+environmental+redundancy+noise+quantum+classical&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.1007/s44464-026-00025-9\", \"title\": [\"Representational efficiency and noise robustness in hybrid quantum-classical graph neural networks\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/s44464-026-00025-9\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 7, 23]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1142/s0219477505002811\", \"title\": [\"ROBUSTNESS VERSUS REDUNDANCY IN BIOLOGICAL SYSTEMS\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p> Genetic networks offer a wealth of data; this is mainly due to the genomic dimensionality rather than the samples, as the latter usually come from measurements obtained under a few experimental conditions or time points. It is therefore a challenging task to design suitable statistical models and to develop effective reverse engineering algorithms. The signature of noise is pervasive in genetic networks. For instance, in perturbation experiments only a few genes change expression value, while most genes are either noisy or constant. Consequently, a genetic regulatory network is a redundant system, due to the high-dimensionality and the dependence between genes, and also a sparse system through the gene-gene interaction matrix only partially active. In order to explore these two aspects, redundancy and sparsity, independent component analysis (ICA) is proposed as a flexible approximation model targeted to dimensionality reduction and gene feature selection. </jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1142/s0219477505002811\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2005, 9]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1088/1361-6382/aeb25a\", \"title\": [\"Observer-robust energy condition verification for warp drive spacetimes\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>\\n                  <jats:p>Energy-condition tests for warp-drive spacetimes must account for all admissible causal directions at each point. We use the classical S-lemma to express the null, weak and strong conditions as 4×4 linear matrix inequalities; the dominant condition requires two such tests.
